titleStmt.title: A MARTE Subset to Enable Application-Platform Co-simulation and Schedulability Analysis of NoCbased Embedded Systems

analytic.title: A MARTE Subset to Enable Application-Platform Co-simulation and Schedulability Analysis of NoCbased Embedded Systems

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: MARTE has matured into a substantial industrially relevant profile that extends UML expressive power to support the specification and design of embedded systems. When supported by appropriate model transformation and code generation tools, MARTE forms an appropriate starting point for embedded system development.. In this paper we propose a simpler yet less powerful subset of MARTE, targeted at multiprocessor systems and amenable to early analysis (including timing) of design alternatives before committing to a particular design for implementation. We use the proposed subset of MARTE constructs to generate abstract simulation and real-time schedulability analysis models, allowing both average and worstcase performance metrics to be considered when comparing multiple design alternatives.

div.head: INTRODUCTION
div.p: At the core of the design process of multiprocessor embedded systems, designers search over different platform configurations for the one that would better meet the constraints imposed on the system by its application domain, e.g. power, space, and for real-time embedded systems, time. Configuration points include number of processing cores, type of interconnect, task allocation policies, arbitration, among others. Model-driven methodologies are known for supporting that process by allowing designers to specify templates of platforms and respective configuration alternatives, which are then used to automatically generate multiple system prototypes that can be comparatively evaluated, hoping that at least one of them would satisfy all application constraints.

A survey over the state-of-the-art (including [1][2] [3]) shows that many model-based approaches to multiprocessor embedded systems design use UML-based specification languages such as MARTE [4] to describe system platform, application functionality and their respective configurations. Then, the UML specifications are used to generate a number of alternate system implementations that can be comparatively evaluated. Most approaches use (part of) the UML specification as input to code generation tools that output programming language code (from the specification of the application functionality) and hardware description language (HDL) code (from the specification of the hardware platform).

While producing very accurate evaluation results, and as consequence a fair comparison between design alternatives, this process can be very time consuming: evaluating one second of application target time can take several hours [5]. An obvious disadvantage of this approach is that the excessive evaluation time limits the number N of alternatives that can be considered. This is illustrated in Figure 1(a), classified as an implementation based design approach. In this paper, we follow a different approach by allowing search and evaluation of design alternatives before the generation and prototyping of the actual hardware and software components of the system. This is illustrated in Figure 1(b), classified as an abstract-model based design approach. Essentially, from the UML we use model transformation techniques to generate and evaluate abstract models of the system. This allows us to evaluate a larger set M of alternatives, and then choose only the N best ones to be implemented and evaluated (e.g. through cycle-accurate simulation or actual execution on an FPGA).

Within this paper, we consider abstract model-based design exploration for real-time embedded systems targeted at multiprocessors based on networks-on-chip (NoC). Typically, such systems have important application constraints that are notoriously hard to evaluate (e.g. inter-task communication latency over the interconnect network, application time deadlines), and because their complexity makes the evaluation at the cycle-accurate level infeasible as the number of cores increase. By choosing such complex architectures as our main target, we hope to show that the approach would also be applicable to simpler systems.
The main contributions of the paper are the following:

definition of a MARTE subset for modelling of the realtime embedded system application functionality and platform configuration points for NoC-based multiprocessors; -definition of intermediate models that are appropriate for the evaluation and analysis of specific configurations before generating HDL and programming language code.

For the first contribution, we show that the proposed subset is sufficiently rich to enable early system performance evaluation. For the second contribution, we use model transformation to generate evaluation models based on existing real-time analysis and abstract simulation techniques.

div.head: II. COMPARISON WITH RELATED WORK
div.p: As outlined in Section I, a number of UML-based techniques have been proposed to support the design of multiprocessor embedded systems. Some rely upon direct code generation of hardware or software components out of UML diagrams [6] [7]. However, most approaches allow exploration of the application-platform mapping space following Gajski's Y-chart methodology, as described within a model-driven engineering (MDE) context by Dekeyser et al in [8]. Below, we focus on research following the MDE methodology.

In [1], Kangas et al describe a sophisticated framework that allows the complete generation of hardware and software components of a multiprocessor system. They rely on a significant portion of the UML 2 standard to model the complete functionality of the application as well as the detailed platform architecture [9]. Such models are then used to generate programming language source and HDL code. Following the MoPCoM methodology [10], Vidal et al used a different subset of UML 2 to generate source and HDL [3] and then extended that approach to support dynamically reconfigurable co-processors and accelerators [11]. Dekeyser et al reported in [2] the use of several model transformation techniques within the Gaspard2 framework to generate SystemC, OpenMP Fortran and VHDL code from MARTE models, aiming to prototype complete MPSoC systems. Mueller et al described the SATURN approach in [12], which aims at closing the gap between SysML models and the generation of C/C++ and synthesisable SystemC code. Validation of design alternatives are based on co-simulation of hardware components modelled in SystemC and targetcompiled software components executed over the QEMU emulator.

All those approaches have common features: design space exploration is done manually or using static analysis; the goal is to automatically generate implementation-level source code and HDL; evaluation of a particular design alternative can only be done once implementation-level code has been generated.

The approach presented in this paper has a different goal. It does not aim to support the complete implementation of the system, and it focuses only on the early design space exploration and evaluation of design alternatives before the actual prototyping. It proposes the transformation of the UMLbased specification model into different intermediate models that are unable to generate an implementation but can be used to effectively compare different design alternatives. Such models can guide the design exploration process in a way that poor design alternatives can be identified and discarded with minor design effort. Furthermore, intermediate models do not include a detailed specification of application and platform functionality and are based on a small set of modelling constructs. This increases the appeal and adoption potential of this approach by designers, as it offers a simpler -yet less powerful -alternative to UML 2, MARTE or SysML. Obviously, once a set of suitable design alternatives is found using our approach, there still is a need for the approaches reviewed above in order to increment the models so that a complete implementation can be generated (Figure 1).

Other approaches using UML-derived intermediate models to support early evaluation of design alternatives include [13], [14] and the Execution Modeling Level (EML) part of the MoPCoM methodology [10]. In this paper we significantly extend the state of the art by supporting both static and executable intermediate models, and by considering more complex platforms i.e. large multicores with NoC interconnects.

div.head: III. PROPOSED APPROACH
div.p: The following subsections directly address the contributions stated in Section I.

div.head: A. Proposed Modelling Language
div.p: The proposed language is a subset of the MARTE UML profile. MARTE was designed to support many aspects of different design styles and has expanded into a very powerful but also very complex language covering many diverse aspects of systems. It is common sense among MARTE users that the profile has several different ways to describe the same concept. One of the contributions of this paper is to delimit a minimal set of modelling constructs that can enable the design space exploration of NoC-based embedded real-time systems. The proposed subset is shown in Table I.

To model applications, we propose two views that complement each other on the description of structure and behaviour. The structural constructs are mainly chosen from MARTE High Level Application Modelling (HLAM) and Generic Component Model (GCM) packages. With those constructs, designers can describe application tasks and the abstract channels through which they communicate. Behavioural constructs such as periodicity of tasks and communication, jitter, deadlines and priorities use HLAM realtime feature specification. Other quantitative constraints are selected from the Generic Quantitative Analysis Modelling package (GQAM).

Platform modelling uses constructs from the Generic Resource Modelling (GRM) and Hardware Resource Modelling (HRM) packages of MARTE, which allow the creation of composites using any configuration of processing cores, caches, buffers and interconnects. The behaviour of platforms uses schedulers from GRM and arbiters from HRM, as well as and discrete clocks from the Time package. To enable the reuse of existing simulation models, platforms can also be described using configurations, as in [15]. That way, designers can quickly define a platform model by setting parameters of a "HeMPS" [16] or a "PurplePringle" [17] configuration, which would then be transformed into simulation models, respectively, of a multicore platform based on the HERMES NoC or on a priority-preemptive NoC.

div.head: B. Abstract Simulation Infrastructure
div.p: As intended, the proposed profile cannot be used to generate a prototype or even a cycle-accurate simulation model of a multiprocessor embedded system. However, it contains sufficient information to derive an abstract simulation model that is accurate enough to enable the comparison of different design alternatives. Such abstract simulation models can be orders of magnitude faster than cycle-accurate models [17], so that more alternatives can be evaluated.

We now define the type of abstract simulation models we use within the proposed work. Our models abstract away some information about the application, i.e. the sequences of instructions that compose a particular application task, or the data words that compose a particular communication message. Instead, they represent the time it takes to execute that sequence of instructions over a particular processor, or the time it takes to transfer those data words over a particular communication channel. Such level of abstraction is often referred as loosely-timed within Transaction-Level Modelling (TLM) 2.0 taxonomy. According to the accepted level of accuracy loss, those time representations can be a single value (e.g. the task will always execute in 5ms), a probability distribution function, or a series of predefined values (e.g. from execution traces). Such models can be easily derived from an application described using the MARTE subset proposed in subsection III.A, and can be used to simulate the load imposed by an application to a particular platform. It is important to notice that the platform model does not necessarily have to follow the same level of abstraction that we impose for the application. Abstract models of applications can be used, for instance, to drive approximately-timed or cycle-accurate platform models. However, the greatest benefits in terms of evaluation speed can be obtained if the platform model is also defined at an abstract level. Therefore, in this work we rely on approximately-timed TLM to describe platforms models that allow the exploration of the trade-off between fast evaluation and high accuracy. The actual model libraries are not the focus of this paper, so we reuse the work from [18] and [17] to co-simulate loosely-timed models of concurrent applications and approximately-timed NoC-based platform models. The co-simulation of those models provides us with the response time of each task as well as the communication latency of each message over the NoC. Those figures can be aggregated into end-to-end latencies and used to evaluate the average application performance and the best/worst observed cases.

div.head: C. Schedulability Analysis
div.p: For real-time embedded systems, it is often necessary to bound the worst-case performance of the system. Bounds are usually described as deadlines on the completion of software task executions and message transmissions. Using simulation, it is only possible to determine if those deadlines are met within the simulated scenarios -there is no guarantee that the worst case behaviour of all tasks and messages can be identified through simulation.

To complement the simulation-based evaluation described in the previous subsection, real-time schedulability analysis models can be generated from the proposed MARTE subset. These are used to generate schedulability analysis models that can evaluate whether tasks and messages will always meet their deadlines even in the worst case scenarios (which may or may not be uncovered through simulation). The analysis calculates the worst-case response times of fixed priority tasks given an allocation of tasks to processor cores, and the worst case latency of messages transmitted over of wormhole NoCs using recent developments reported in [19].

Within the abstract model-driven design approach used within this paper, schedulability analysis is actually performed using the timing characteristics of the models, as specified within the MARTE description (e.g. the MARTE subset allows the definition of task deadlines, periods etc). Subsequently, when the actual system software is generated and compiled, it is necessary only to check that the worst-case execution times of the compiled software processes are no greater than specified in the model.

Within the toolset supporting our abstract model-driven approach, a library implementing the schedulability analysis was specially created. This can be customised according to application and platform models that follow the proposed MARTE subset. The analytical models output the worst-case response time of each task as well as the worst-case communication latency over the NoC interconnect. This enables the evaluation of end-to-end latencies: tasks and their respective inter-task communication messages. This is done by assuming that tasks execute first and then communicate, and by considering the variation of the response time of the originating task as jitter over the respective communication messages. If the worst case end-to-end latency of each task communication (which includes the latency of its source and destination tasks) is less than its respective deadline, the system is said to be schedulable.

div.head: IV. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
div.p: To validate the proposed approach, we used the modelling constructs on Table I to specify an autonomous vehicle application, a NoC-based homogeneous multiprocessor platform and different policies for allocating application tasks onto platform processing cores.

The autonomous vehicle (AV) application was introduced in [20] and comprehends 33 sporadic tasks (referred by fourcharacter acronyms, e.g. VIBS) and 39 inter-task communication messages (referred by their number). It includes functionality such as navigation control, vibration control and obstacle detection through stereo photogrammetry. Tasks and messages were characterised using the constructs marked with "A" in Table I. For each task, the execution time was considered to be its worst-case execution time (WCET) on the platform processing core, and its deadline was considered to be its period.

The platform was characterised using the constructs marked with "P" in Table I, including number of processors, operating frequency, type of task scheduler on each processor, interconnect topology and size, type of interconnect arbitration, interconnect link throughput and interconnect routing scheme. Our libraries support the generation and simulation of several design alternatives, but to simplify the analysis of results we had to restrict some of the dimensions of the design space. Therefore, all experiments presented here assume homogeneous multicore platforms with priority-preemptive task schedulers, 2D-mesh NoC interconnects with XY dimension routing, credit-based flow control, 8 virtual channels with 2-flit input buffers per port and priority-preemptive link arbitration. But both the proposed language and intermediate simulation models would support alternatives on each and every of those design choices. The static analysis we use from [19] also allows flexibility on routing, buffering and flow control, but priority-preemptive arbitration is a requirement.
Figure 2 shows parts of the MARTE diagrams used for application and platform modelling.

To mimic a typical design space exploration flow, our goal in this experiment is to find a platform configuration and a task allocation that meet the constraints of the AV application. Our models support any possible allocation of tasks onto processors, but as the number of possible allocations increases factorially with the number of tasks and processors, it is unfeasible to do an exhaustive search. We therefore restrict the possible platform configurations to 3x3, 4x4 and 5x5 topologies, and we use a genetic algorithm (GA) to search for allocations over each one of those configurations, as follows:

we generate a schedulability analysis model of the AV application and a 3x3 platform as described in subsection III.C, using an arbitrary allocation of tasks to cores; -we feed the generated model to the GA, which uses mutation and crossover operations (randomly swapping and reallocating tasks) to derive a generation of 100 new allocations;

our schedulability analysis library is then used to evaluate, for each allocation, whether each task execution and communication is schedulable, i.e. would meet the respective deadline in the worst-case scenario; all allocations are ranked according to a metric U which represents how many unschedulable tasks and communication each allocation produces; -those allocations with a higher than average value of U are discarded, while the remaining are used as basis for the next generation; the algorithm iterates until it finds an allocation with U=0 or until it reaches 300 generations (that is, a total of 30000 allocations); -this process is repeated for the 4x4 and 5x5 platforms.

Table II shows the number of schedulable allocations found by our GA in 10 runs of the algorithm for each platform. The average value of U over the 10 runs is also shown. We then discarded the 3x3 and 5x5 platforms, as we could not find a suitable allocation on the former and could find more efficient allocations than those on the latter. Once established that a 4x4 topology would be the best alternative for the AV application, we looked more carefully at different alternatives on task allocation. Table III shows three different allocations A1, A2 and A3. Allocation A1 is the one used in [20], while allocations A2 and A3 were found using the genetic algorithm described above (and therefore found to be schedulable by our analysis model). 3.b and 3.c show the worst case end-to-end latencies for allocations A1, A2 and A3 respectively. The values for each of the 39 inter-task communications are plotted with a brown cross and were obtained using our intermediate schedulability analysis model. We have a confirmation that A2 and A3 have U=0 and are schedulable, as all worst case latencies are less than the respective deadlines, shown as a red horizontal line. A1, however, has a number of unschedulable communications, denoted by the brown crosses plotted at the upper margin of Figure 3.a (the actual worst case latencies in those cases are undetermined, as our analysis model stops iterating towards a solution once a deadline is missed). To better discriminate the allocation policies, we generate abstract simulation models of the application and platform as described in subsection III.B. We simulate each scenario for a target time of 200 seconds, which allows for a good coverage of the application lifetime (the shortest period is of the video processing tasks, that must execute every 0.04 seconds to achieve 25 VGA frames per second, and the longest period is of 1 second for the tyre pressure control task). Figure 3 also shows, for each allocation, the best, worst and average end-toend latency of the 39 inter-task communications. The plots show that allocation A2 produced communications with worst case and maximum observed latencies that are very close to the respective deadlines (specially in communications 4, 7 and 37). Taking that into account, allocation A3 would be preferable as its results allow for larger margins.

div.head: V. CONCLUSIONS
div.p: This paper has identified a MARTE subset which enables the generation of intermediate models that can be used for fast design space exploration at early stages of the multiprocessor embedded systems design flow. The presented work has concentrated on intermediate models based on real-time schedulability analysis and abstract TLM simulation, showing that the proposed subset was sufficiently expressive to enable the generation of both types of intermediate models.

The proposed approach can be used on its own or on top of other MARTE-based flows that enable full system implementation such as [1] and [2]. Its main advantage is to allow fast model construction and analysis, so that a larger number of design alternatives can be evaluated before committing to a specific implementation. For example, in the presented experiment our approach was used to evaluate up to 30000 different task allocations for each platform alternative (3x3, 4x4 and 5x5), which would certainly be infeasible with cycle-accurate implementations. Similar abstract models could have been used to evaluate both performance and energy consumption as in [21], but energy metrics were not considered in this paper and the proposal of a UML/MARTE extension for low-power multicores is left for future work.
